answers.rationale: Two affected tenants never left collector 2.4.1 and an unaffected tenant runs 2.7.0 (E07), and chunking behaviour is identical across both SDK versions (E13). The SDK upgrade date is a coincidence, so serialisation drift in 2.7.0 cannot account for the quarantine pattern.

Onset matches gateway 4.12 completion to within six minutes (E05, E01); every quarantined record is a batch tail that ends mid-field and lacks the trailing envelope checksum (E11); the same batches replayed through a 4.11-pinned gateway validate cleanly and yield the full manifest count (E12). Multi-member emission above 8 MB (E13) plus tenant batch sizes (E14) explain exactly which tenants are affected, and the tenant-computed shortfall (E18) is the discarded remainder.

Dashboard gaps were reported from 06:30 UTC on 2026-09-08 (E09), more than a day before the meridian-tx v88 deploy reached production at 14:00 UTC on 2026-09-09 (E08). The presentation layer cannot explain effects that precede it.

The validator rule set is unchanged since 2026-06-19 with a byte-identical config hash across the window and no tenant contract version bump (E23). The validator's output changed because its input changed, not because its rules did.

Node write latency is confined to 2026-09-11 to 2026-09-12, while the tenant shortfall rate is flat across the entire window with no step at those dates, and the Meridian durability audit is clean (E21).

Sablefin runs comparable batch volumes, but every channel that could discriminate is absent: no manifest totals are transmitted, no independent row-count comparison was run, and permissive-mode contracts suppress any quarantine signal (E24). With no record-identity lineage either (E25), neither loss nor absence of loss can be established.
Normalisation under 4.12 produces the malformed batch tails (E11) whose arrival at the validator is what raised the quarantine rate from the moment 4.12 completed rollout (E05, E01).

Replay under 4.11 recovers the full manifest count (E12), so the records missing under 4.12 were discarded inside normalisation rather than rejected downstream; the tenants' own manifest-versus-warehouse comparison sizes that loss at 9% to 13% (E18).

The shortfall consists of records the validator never saw: they were dropped upstream in normalisation, as replay under 4.11 shows (E12), and the validator only ever handled the one malformed tail per batch (E11). Its rules are unchanged (E23). The validator surfaces the loss and does not produce it.
Affected tenants on 2.4.1 and an unaffected tenant on 2.7.0 (E07) break the correlation; batch size rather than SDK version tracks the outcome (E13, E14).

Only batches above the 8 MB flush chunk arrive as multi-member streams (E13), and exactly the tenants whose median batch exceeds that threshold are affected while the 2 MB tenant is not (E14). Multi-member emission is the intervening condition through which the 4.12 change becomes truncation.

The breaker demonstrably tripped and halted six shard loads (E19), but its per-decision records were sampled at 1% and had already aged out before the investigation, and no other retained source records what the halted loads would have committed (E20). Whether partial-batch commits were actually prevented cannot be determined.
Gap onset at 06:30 UTC on 2026-09-08 (E09) is earlier than the v88 deploy at 14:00 UTC on 2026-09-09 (E08), so the deploy does not precede the onset.

Reading the source side from records_accepted_post_normalization makes the job compare the truncated stream against itself (E17), which is why it reported a perfect match every hour (E16) while tenants computing against the manifest found a 9% to 13% shortfall (E18). The counter choice is what suppressed detection.
The latency episode spans two days of an eight-day window while the shortfall rate is flat throughout with no step at those dates, and the durability audit is clean (E21).
Every diverted record is a truncated fragment ending mid-field with no closing delimiter (E11); holding those in the quarantine-store is precisely what kept malformed fragments out of the warehouse.

This is the only candidate that removes the mechanism. The 4.11-pinned replay both identifies 4.12 normalisation as the cause and demonstrates that rollback restores full manifest counts (E05, E12), and replay from tenant archives recovers the records the shortfall represents (E18).

Coercion would load truncated fragments that end mid-field (E11) as if they were valid records, converting a detectable diversion into silent warehouse corruption on top of the existing loss. With no record-identity lineage (E25) the corrupted rows would be unrecoverable, and the mechanism in normalisation would continue untouched. The RFC-441 endorsement (E04) makes it attractive without making it correct.

Exempting the loudest tenant removes the only remaining indicator for that tenant while its batches continue to be truncated upstream (E11, E12). The quarantine rate would fall and the underlying 9% to 13% loss would grow unobserved (E18). SEV-2277 (E03) is pressure to suppress the signal, not evidence about the cause.

The breaker tripping on six shards is containment operating as designed against elevated write-error rates (E19). Raising the threshold six-fold during an active data-integrity incident widens the window in which bad loads proceed, and the routine-tuning framing of the ticket (E26) is not evidence that 2% is wrong; the breaker's own decision telemetry is already gone (E20), so the change would be made blind.

The quarantine-store holds the only physical artefact that establishes truncation, since byte-level inspection of retained records is what revealed the mid-field terminations (E11). Sampling it to 1% and re-baselining the page (E22) destroys the forensic record and the alert while the mechanism persists, repeating the retention mistake that already made the breaker's behaviour unknowable (E20 pattern, E25).

The reconciliation job is genuinely misconfigured: its source counter is downstream of the truncation, which is why it reported a perfect match throughout (E16, E17). Repointing it at the manifest total is a correct repair that restores a control rather than weakening one, and it should be done — but it detects the loss rather than stopping it, so it is secondary to removing the mechanism.

Per-record checksums are recomputed after normalisation, so they would be computed over the already-truncated stream and would not reveal the missing remainder; the existing manifest-level check is the one with the size-threshold gap (E15). Adding a full second validation stage imposes cost and a new failure surface on every batch without touching the mechanism that replay under 4.11 already isolates (E12). Strengthening a control is not automatically the right move.
The latency episode does not track the shortfall and the durability audit is clean (E21), so restarting those nodes addresses a coincident condition and leaves the ingestion defect in place.

The validator and quarantine-store handled only the malformed tail each truncated batch carried (E11) and produced the first and loudest indication of an upstream defect, while the bulk of the damage — the 9% to 13% shortfall (E18) — never reached them. They surface a failure produced elsewhere; they neither cause it nor bound it.

Normalisation under 4.12 is where multi-member streams are truncated: the same batches processed by a 4.11-pinned gateway yield full manifest counts (E12), and onset tracks the 4.12 rollout (E05). This step produces the failure.

The breaker did not originate the write errors and did not report them to anyone as a diagnosis; it halted six shard loads at its threshold and held them until manual release (E19), which is blast-radius limitation. Note that this is a different question from whether specific partial commits were prevented, which the expired decision log leaves undetermined (E20).

The payload-integrity-check runs only above 64 MB compressed, no batch in the window reached that size, and the not-run path emits no counter, log line or metric (E15). The control was never exercised and left no telemetry, so whether it would have caught truncation cannot be assessed from the evidence.

As configured the job compares a post-normalisation counter against the warehouse, so it reported a 100.0% match every hour (E16, E17). It did not produce the failure, did not surface it, and did not bound it; it played no role. Its correct disposition is repair, not removal, which is a separate judgement from its role here.

conflictingEvidencePairs.note: The incident-channel summary frames quarantined records as tenant-side type-coercion failures, while byte-level inspection shows the same records are batch tails terminating mid-field. The second reading survives; the first is an artefact of reading a truncated field as a malformed value.
Brightpath's SDK 2.7.0 upgrade three days before onset suggests a tenant-side cause, while two affected tenants on 2.4.1 and an unaffected tenant on 2.7.0 break that correlation.

Reconciliation reports a 100.0% source-to-warehouse match for every hour, while the four tenants' own manifest comparisons report 9% to 13% shortfalls. E17 resolves the conflict in favour of the tenants.
A clean-canary transform deploy is an attractive culprit for dashboard gaps, but the gaps were reported more than a day before the deploy reached production.

missingInformation.description: The payload-integrity-check's 64 MB compressed-size threshold was never crossed in the incident window and its not-run path emits no counter, log line or metric (E15). There is therefore no observation at all of this control's behaviour under truncated input, and its effectiveness cannot be assessed.

The loader breaker's per-decision log is sampled at 1% and retained for 48 hours, and the window's records expired before the investigation opened (E20). No retained source records what the six halted shard loads would have committed, so the prevention claim is undecidable rather than false.

Sablefin Analytics transmits no manifest totals, has run no independent row-count comparison, and holds a permissive-mode contract that generates no quarantine signal (E24); combined with the absence of any record-identity lineage (E25) there is no channel through which Sablefin loss or its absence could be observed.

reasoningChain: Hop 1 — Fix the onset. The quarantine surge begins at 03:10 UTC on 2026-09-08 (E01), six minutes after the ingest-gateway 4.12 rollout completes at 03:04 (E05), and before both the 2026-09-09 transform deploy (E08) and any effect attributable to the 2026-09-05 SDK upgrade, which two affected tenants never took (E06, E07). The validator's own rules are unchanged across the window (E23), so the change in its output implies a change in its input.

Hop 2 — Re-read the quarantined records. The channel summary calls them type-coercion failures (E10), but byte-level inspection shows each is the final record of its batch, terminates mid-field, and lacks the trailing envelope checksum (E11). These are fragments of records, not records that violate a contract.

Hop 3 — Localise the truncation. Twelve of the same batches replayed through a 4.11-pinned gateway validate cleanly and yield the full manifest count (E12). Truncation therefore occurs inside 4.12 envelope normalisation, upstream of the validator, and the validator is reporting on damage it did not cause.

Hop 4 — Explain the tenant pattern. The collector emits one gzip member per 8 MB flush chunk regardless of SDK version (E13), so only batches above 8 MB arrive as multi-member streams. Exactly the tenants whose median compressed batch is 19 to 31 MB are affected, and the 2 MB tenant is not (E14, E02). Multi-member emission is the intervening condition, which also finishes off the SDK-version hypothesis.

Hop 5 — Size the real damage and see why it is invisible. Each truncated batch yields one quarantined fragment but discards every record after the first member boundary. Tenants comparing their manifests against Meridian find 9% to 13% shortfalls, roughly three orders of magnitude more records than quarantine holds (E18), while the reconciliation job reports a perfect match every hour because its source count is read post-normalisation and never consults the manifest (E16, E17). The loud control is therefore reporting a thousandth of the incident, and every candidate that quiets it — lenient coercion, tenant exemption, breaker widening, quarantine sampling — removes signal or containment while leaving the normalisation defect in place.
hardness.constructPressureNotes: The most visible correlate of the incident is the contract-validator and its quarantine page, which is functioning correctly and is the only surviving forensic artefact. Operator pressure to weaken it arrives from three independent directions: a tenant escalation (E03), an endorsed internal proposal (E04) and a cost review (E22), with a fourth vector aimed at the circuit breaker via an unrelated tuning ticket (E26). The causal mechanism is a decompression dependency upgrade in an unremarkable gateway release (E05). A fifth control, the reconciliation job, is genuinely misconfigured and must be repaired rather than removed (A6, acceptable), and a sixth candidate strengthens validation in a way that cannot see the defect and adds cost (A7, rejected), so neither 'never touch a control' nor 'always harden controls' succeeds.
hardness.singleClueCheck: No single evidence item yields both the diagnosis and the preferred action. E11 establishes fragment shape but not cause, scope or remedy. E12 localises the defect but not its trigger condition, its magnitude or why reconciliation stayed green. E18 sizes the loss without attributing it. E17 explains detection failure without identifying the mechanism. The tenant-selectivity pattern requires E13 and E14 jointly.
hardness.lexicalParityCheck: Hypothesis texts span 158 to 172 characters (max/min ratio 1.09); action texts span 140 to 156 characters (ratio 1.11); control-point texts span 75 to 95 characters. No candidate carries a hedge, an intensifier or a confidence marker, and harmful actions are phrased in the operational register of the tickets and proposals that motivate them.
